units.title: The Skeletal System
units.intro: Bone is living: hard matrix (calcium salts) + collagen + cells. Compact bone outside, spongy inside, marrow in the middle (blood cells). Cartilage cushions; ligaments bone-to-bone.

f2.title: Axial = skull + spine + ribs. Appendicular = girdles + limbs.

cards.title: Axial = skull + spine + ribs. Appendicular = girdles + limbs.
3.1.1 Structure and Composition of Bone
body: A bone begins as cartilage before it is converted to bone through a process called ossification.
The key players in bone development are cartilage cells and mature bone cells.
Cut the bones into cross-sectional and longitudinal halves. c.
Examine the internal structure of the bones.

cards.title: 3.1.2 Cartilage and Ligaments
body: **Cartilage** is a type of connective tissue consisting of a tough, flexible matrix made of collagen, protein, and sugar.
Although not as hard as a bone, cartilage forms an important structural component of many parts of the skeletal system.
Much of the fetal skeleton is formed entirely of cartilage.
Cartilage exists in several forms, from glassy to fibrous in appearance.

cards.title: 3.1.3 Axial and appendicular skeletons — the two halves of the body’s frame
body: **Step 1 — the big split.** The human skeleton (about **206 bones** in an adult) is divided into two parts: the **axial skeleton** (80 bones) and the **appendicular skeleton** (126 bones).

**Step 2 — axial = the axis.** Picture a line down the middle of your body. The bones **on that central axis** form the axial skeleton: **skull, vertebral column (backbone) and thorax (sternum + ribs)**.

**Step 3 — appendicular = the appendages.** Bones **hanging from** (appended to) that axis — the **limbs (arms and legs)** and the **girdles** that join them to the axis — form the appendicular skeleton.

**Step 4 — the jobs differ.** Axial: mainly **protection** of vital organs (brain, spinal cord, heart, lungs) and a **central framework**. Appendicular: mainly **movement** and handling objects; the girdles give the limbs their wide range of movement.
**Step 5 — where they meet.** The two parts join at the **shoulders** (pectoral girdle ↔ sternum) and the **hips** (pelvic girdle ↔ sacrum).

steps.text: **Axial skeleton = 80 bones:** skull 22, ear ossicles 6, hyoid 1, vertebral column 26, sternum 1, ribs 24.
**Appendicular skeleton = 126 bones:** pectoral girdle 4, arms 60, pelvic girdle 2, legs 60.
The textbook counts 8 cranial + 14 facial bones + 3 tiny bones in each ear. The **hyoid** (a U-shaped bone in the neck that holds the tongue) completes the 80.

cards.title: A. The axial skeleton — skull
body: **Cranium (8 bones):** a strong bony box that **protects the brain**. It has small holes (perforations) through which **blood vessels and nerves** pass to and from the brain.

**Facial bones (14):** include the **upper jaw (maxilla)** and the **lower jaw (mandible)** — the only skull bone that moves (for chewing and speaking). The skull also protects the **olfactory organs (nose), the middle and inner ear and the eyes** (eye sockets).
**Ear ossicles (3 in each ear):** malleus, incus, stapes — the smallest bones in the body; they pass sound vibrations to the inner ear.

**Sutures and fontanels:** the skull bones are tightly fitted together by immovable joints (sutures). At birth many are not yet joined, leaving **“soft spots” (fontanels)** that let the skull squeeze slightly during birth and let the brain grow. They close by about **two years** of age.

cards.title: The vertebral column (backbone)
body: **Length and number:** about **70 cm** long in an adult. It is made of **33 vertebrae** in a child; in the adult the lower ones fuse, so there are **26 separate bones** (24 vertebrae + sacrum + coccyx).
**Discs of cartilage** lie between the vertebrae. They **absorb shock, reduce friction** and let the column **bend** a little at each joint — together this gives a flexible backbone.

**Three jobs:** (1) the **main support** from which the rest of the upper body branches; (2) **protects the spinal cord** (and spinal nerves) inside the vertebral canal; (3) gives **attachment** for ribs and back muscles.

**Atlas and axis:** the first two cervical vertebrae are special. The **atlas (C1)** carries the skull and allows **nodding** (“yes”); the **axis (C2)** has a peg on which the atlas turns, allowing **rotation** (“no”).
**Caudal vertebrae** vary between animals with the size of the tail. In humans the tail is **vestigial**, so the four caudal vertebrae fuse to form the **coccyx**.

cards.title: The five regions of the vertebral column

steps.text: **Cervical — 7** (neck). Atlas and axis move the head.
**Thoracic — 12** (chest). Each carries a pair of ribs.
**Lumbar — 5** (lower back). Largest and strongest, carry most body weight.
**Sacral — 5 fused → sacrum.** Joins the pelvic girdle.
**Caudal (coccygeal) — 4 fused → coccyx.** Remnant of a tail.

cards.title: Memory hook — vertebrae per region: “breakfast at 7, lunch at 12, dinner at 5”
body: Cervical 7 → Thoracic 12 → Lumbar 5, then Sacral 5 and Caudal 4. Say “7-12-5-5-4” like a phone number.

cards.title: The thorax — sternum and ribs
body: **Sternum (breastbone):** a flat bone about **15 cm** long in the middle of the chest.

**Ribs:** **12 pairs** (24 ribs). Every pair joins a thoracic vertebra at the back. Their main purpose is to **protect the heart and lungs**; their **cartilage** joints make the rib cage **flexible for breathing**.
**True ribs — upper 7 pairs:** joined **directly** to the sternum by their own cartilage.
**False ribs — next 3 pairs (8–10):** joined **indirectly** — their cartilage joins the cartilage of the rib above.

**Floating ribs — last 2 pairs (11–12):** **not attached to the sternum at all**; they are fixed only to the vertebrae at the back. (The textbook’s wording “the sternum is connected to all ribs except the last pair” and “attached to the last pair of ribs” is loose — remember **7 true, 3 false, 2 floating**.)

cards.title: B. The appendicular skeleton — girdles
body: **What it is:** the bones of the **appendages (limbs)** and the **girdles** that attach them to the axial skeleton.

**Pectoral (shoulder) girdle — 4 bones:** two **scapulae** (shoulder blades) and two **clavicles** (collar bones). It forms a **loose attachment** with the sternum, which lets the arms move very freely. The **scapula** rests on the back of the rib cage and gives a **broad flat surface** for arm muscles and a **socket** for the head of the humerus. The **clavicle** props the shoulder outwards and **stops it collapsing inward**.

**Pelvic (hip) girdle — 2 hip bones:** each hip bone is several bones (ilium, ischium, pubis) **fused together**; with the sacrum they form a strong **ring**. Its functions: (1) **socket** for the femur, (2) surface for **muscle attachment**, (3) **protects** lower abdominal organs (bladder, reproductive organs), (4) **transmits body weight** from the backbone to the legs.
**Why the difference?** The shoulder girdle is light and loose → **range of movement**. The hip girdle is heavy and fused → **strength and weight bearing**.

cards.title: i. The upper appendages — arm and hand (30 bones each)
body: **Upper arm — humerus (1):** the single long bone from shoulder to elbow.

**Forearm — radius and ulna (2):** the **ulna** forms the elbow joint with the humerus; the **radius** is on the **thumb side**. Two bones instead of one allow the forearm and wrist to **twist** (turn the palm up and down).
**Wrist — carpals (8):** small bones in **two irregular rows** joined by **gliding joints**, giving the wrist flexibility.
**Palm — metacarpals (5):** extend from the wrist; covered with skin they form the palm.
**Fingers — phalanges (14):** the **thumb has 2**, each other finger **3** (2 + 4×3 = 14). Phalanges are **long bones** (long in shape, though small).

**The opposable thumb:** the first metacarpal joins the wrist by a **saddle joint** while the others lie in one plane. So the thumb can swing across to touch each fingertip — letting humans **grasp objects, use tools and do skilful work**. This is one feature that makes the human skeleton unique.

cards.title: ii. The lower appendages — leg and foot (30 bones each)
body: **Thigh — femur (1):** the upper bone of the leg; the **longest, largest and strongest** bone of the body.
**Knee cap — patella (1):** a thick bone in the tendon in front of the knee; it **covers and protects** the front of the knee joint.
**Lower leg — tibia and fibula (2):** connect the femur to the ankle. The **tibia** (shin bone) is the thick, weight-bearing one; the **fibula** is thin, on the outer side.
**Ankle — tarsals (7):** include the heel bone.

**Sole — metatarsals (5).** **Toes — phalanges (14):** 2 in the big toe and 3 in each other toe — the same pattern as the hand, but **much shorter** and (in the first row) flattened sideways. (The textbook says toes are “composed of metatarsals” — the toes are phalanges; the metatarsals form the sole.)
**Foot at a right angle to the leg:** gives a broad, stable base for **standing upright and walking on two legs**.

cards.title: Arm and leg are built on the same plan
head: Part
Arm (upper limb)
Leg (lower limb)

cards.title: Memory hook — limb bones in order: “1-2-many-5-14”
body: Every limb goes **1** long bone → **2** bones → a **cluster** of small bones → **5** long bones → **14** phalanges. The leg adds the patella.

cards.title: Traps examiners love (3.1.3)
body: **Girdles belong to the appendicular skeleton**, not the axial — even though they touch the axis.
**Sternum and ribs are axial**, the clavicle and scapula are appendicular.
**Radius = thumb side; ulna = little-finger side** (forms the elbow).
**Thumb and big toe have 2 phalanges**; all other digits have 3.
**33 vs 26:** 33 vertebrae before fusion; 26 separate bones in an adult.
**Floating ribs** are free at the front — they are not joined to the sternum.

cards.title: Exercise 3.1 Q1
cards.problem: What is the appendicular skeleton? Why is it called appendicular?

steps.text: Step 1: List the bones — limbs (arms, legs) and the girdles (pectoral, pelvic).
Step 2: Explain the name — these bones are **appendages**, “hung onto” (appended to) the central axial skeleton.
Step 3: Add the number — 126 bones.

cards.answer: The appendicular skeleton is the 126 bones of the limbs and their girdles; it is called appendicular because these bones are appendages attached to the axial skeleton.

cards.title: Exercise 3.1 Q2
cards.problem: What is the advantage of the foot forming a right angle to the leg?

steps.text: Step 1: Humans stand and walk upright on two legs (bipedal).
Step 2: A foot at right angles gives a **broad flat base**, so the body is **balanced** and its weight is spread over the sole.
Step 3: The foot acts as a **lever** — the heel strikes and the toes push off — making walking and running efficient.

cards.answer: It provides a broad, stable base for upright posture and balance, spreads body weight, and acts as a lever for walking and running.

cards.title: Exercise 3.1 Q3
cards.problem: Why is the femur the longest, largest and strongest bone of the body?

steps.text: Step 1: The femur carries the **whole weight of the upper body** passed down from the pelvis.
Step 2: It must resist large forces in walking, running and jumping.
Step 3: The most **powerful muscles** of the body (thigh and buttock) attach to it, so it needs a big surface.
Step 4: Its length gives a long stride (long lever).

cards.answer: Because it bears the body’s weight transmitted from the pelvis, withstands the forces of walking and running, gives attachment to the strongest muscles and acts as a long lever.

cards.title: Exercise 3.1 Q4
cards.problem: What are the types of bones found in the human body, as classified by their shapes? Give examples.

steps.text: Step 1: Long bones — longer than wide: femur, humerus, phalanges.
Step 2: Short bones — cube-like: carpals, tarsals.
Step 3: Flat bones — thin plates that protect or anchor muscles: cranial bones, sternum, ribs, scapula.
Step 4: Irregular bones — complex shapes: vertebrae, some facial bones. (The patella is a small bone inside a tendon, often called sesamoid.)

cards.answer: Long, short, flat and irregular bones (e.g. femur; carpals; skull bones and ribs; vertebrae).

cards.title: Count it — the arm
cards.problem: Show that each upper limb has 30 bones and that both upper limbs plus the pectoral girdle make 64.

steps.text: Step 1: Humerus 1 + radius 1 + ulna 1 = 3.
Step 2: Carpals 8 + metacarpals 5 = 13 → running total 16.
Step 3: Phalanges: thumb 2 + 4 fingers × 3 = 14 → 16 + 14 = **30**.
Step 4: Two arms = 60; pectoral girdle = 2 clavicles + 2 scapulae = 4; 60 + 4 = **64**.

cards.title: Apply it — why two forearm bones?
cards.problem: A student turns a door handle and a screwdriver. Which bones make this possible and how?

steps.text: Step 1: Turning the hand palm-up/palm-down needs a twisting forearm.
Step 2: The **radius** rotates around the **ulna**, which stays fixed at the elbow.
Step 3: With a single bone this twisting would be impossible.

cards.answer: The radius rotating around the ulna allows twisting of the forearm and wrist.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which bone belongs to the axial skeleton?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Axial = skull, vertebral column, sternum, ribs.

**Step 2:** Clavicle and scapula are pectoral girdle (appendicular).

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: How many thoracic vertebrae are there?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** 7-12-5-5-4.

**Step 2:** Thoracic = 12, one for each pair of ribs.

**Answer: C.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Ribs 11 and 12 are called floating ribs because they

options.B: are not attached to the sternum

cards.why:
**Step 1:** They are joined to vertebrae at the back.

**Step 2:** At the front they are free — no link to the sternum.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: Quick check

cards.why:
**Step 1:** The other metacarpals lie in one plane.

**Step 2:** The thumb’s saddle joint lets it swing across the palm.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which is a function of the pelvic girdle?

options.B: Transmits body weight from the backbone to the legs

cards.why:
**Step 1:** The pelvic girdle is a strong ring joined to the sacrum.

**Step 2:** It passes the weight of the upper body to the femurs.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Which of the following is an evolutionary advantage of an endoskeleton compared to an exoskeleton?

steps.text: **Step 1: Compare endoskeleton and exoskeleton biology**
An exoskeleton is a non-living outer casing that cannot grow.
Animals with exoskeletons must moult (shed) to grow, during which they are highly vulnerable.
**Step 2: Define endoskeleton characteristics**
An endoskeleton is composed of living tissue that grows continuously alongside the organism's body, eliminating the risky process of moulting.

cards.answer: It grows continuously with the organism, avoiding the need for periodic moulting.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: What is the name of the double-layered fibrous connective tissue membrane that covers the outer surface of a living bone?

steps.text: **Step 1: Identify bone membranes**
The endosteum lines the internal medullary cavities.
The synovial membrane lines articular joint capsules.
**Step 2: Match with outer cover**
The periosteum is the dense, fibrous double-layered membrane that covers the entire outer surface of a bone, supplying it with blood vessels, nerves, and osteoblasts.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following describes the biological function of red bone marrow?

options.A: It stores triglycerides and lipids to serve as chemical energy.
options.B: It is the primary site of hematopoiesis, where blood cells are produced.
options.C: It secretes lubricating synovial fluid into joint cavities.
options.D: It synthesizes calcium and phosphorus crystals.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Contrast marrow types**
Yellow bone marrow stores lipids (fat). Red bone marrow is rich in hematopoietic stem cells.

**Step 2: Identify physiological function**
Red bone marrow continuously produces red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets, a process known as hematopoiesis.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **It is the primary site of hematopoiesis, where blood cells are produced.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What represents the organic matrix of bone, and what mechanical property does it provide?

options.B: Collagen fibers; provides tensile flexibility and strength

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze bone chemical composite**
Bone consists of organic collagen protein fibers and inorganic calcium phosphate salts.

**Step 2: State mechanical functions**
Calcium phosphate provides hardness and compression resistance. Collagen provides flexibility and tensile strength, preventing the bone from shattering easily.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Collagen fibers; provides tensile flexibility and strength**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: One of the following **is not** an organic component of a bone.
cards.why: Calcium phosphate is a mineral salt. It is the **inorganic** part of the bone matrix that provides hardness and strength. Bone cells, nerves, and connective tissues (collagen) are the organic parts.

cards.title: Joints
body: **Joints:** immovable (skull sutures), slightly movable (vertebrae), freely movable synovial (shoulder, knee, hinge elbow). Synovial: capsule + fluid + cartilage. Antagonistic muscles pull across them.

cards.title: Mnemonic
body: Axial is the *axis* you stand on. Appendicular is what you *append* (hang) on the axis.

cards.title: 3.2.1 Movable Joints
body: Ball-and-socket joint: The ball-shaped end of one bone fits into a cup-shaped socket on another.
The ball-and-socket joint allows movement in several directions, including rotation.
Pivot joint: Rounded or conical surfaces of one bone fit into a ring of one or more bones, allowing rotation movement.
An example is the joint between the axis and atlas in the neck.

cards.title: 3.2.2 Immovable Joints
body: Immovable joints exist with bones that are in very close contact and are separated only by a thin layer of fibrous connective tissue.
Joints of the skull are extremely strong and immovable.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following is an evolutionary advantage of an endoskeleton compared to an exoskeleton?

options.A: It provides a completely sealed outer moisture barrier.
options.B: It grows continuously with the organism, avoiding the need for periodic moulting.
options.C: It does not require blood vessels or nutrients.
options.D: It is constructed entirely of non-living, inorganic chitin.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Compare endoskeleton and exoskeleton biology**
An exoskeleton is a non-living outer casing that cannot grow. Animals with exoskeletons must moult (shed) to grow, during which they are highly vulnerable.

**Step 2: Define endoskeleton characteristics**
An endoskeleton is composed of living tissue that grows continuously alongside the organism's body, eliminating the risky process of moulting.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **It grows continuously with the organism, avoiding the need for periodic moulting.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the name of the double-layered fibrous connective tissue membrane that covers the outer surface of a living bone?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify bone membranes**
The endosteum lines the internal medullary cavities. The synovial membrane lines articular joint capsules.

**Step 2: Match with outer cover**
The periosteum is the dense, fibrous double-layered membrane that covers the entire outer surface of a bone, supplying it with blood vessels, nerves, and osteoblasts.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Periosteum**.

cards.title: Joints
body: A **joint** is where two bones meet. **Fixed (immovable):** sutures of the skull. **Slightly movable:** between vertebrae (cartilage discs). **Freely movable (synovial):** have cartilage on the bone ends and a capsule filled with **synovial fluid** that reduces friction. Examples: **ball-and-socket** (shoulder, hip: movement in all directions), **hinge** (elbow, knee: movement in one plane), **pivot** (between the first two neck vertebrae: turning the head), **gliding** (wrist and ankle bones).

cards.title: Step by step: Joints
body: **Step 1:** A joint is where two or more bones meet.
**Step 2:** Immovable (fibrous) joints: bones are fixed by fibrous tissue – sutures of the skull.
**Step 3:** Slightly movable (cartilaginous) joints: bones joined by cartilage pads – between vertebrae, pubic symphysis.
**Step 4:** Freely movable (synovial) joints: a capsule with synovial fluid (lubricant), cartilage on bone ends (reduces friction) and ligaments (join bone to bone).

**Step 5:** Types of synovial joint: ball-and-socket (shoulder, hip – movement in all directions), hinge (elbow, knee – one plane), pivot (atlas–axis, turning the head), gliding (wrist, ankle bones), saddle (thumb).
**Example:** Shoulder vs elbow: the shoulder (ball-and-socket) lets you swing the arm in a full circle; the elbow (hinge) only bends and straightens the forearm like a door.

cards.title: Mnemonic — "Ball Has Pivot Glide Saddle"
body: B-H-P-G-S, the five synovial joints.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: Ligament joins bone to bone; tendon joins muscle to bone. Do not mix them up in joint diagrams.

steps.text: Shoulder or hip.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Evaluate the joint types.
- Fingers and Knee are **hinge joints** (allow movement in one plane).
- Shoulder is a **ball and socket joint** (allows rotation and movement in many planes).
- The joint between the **Atlas and Axis** (the first two neck vertebrae) is a **pivot joint**, which allows the head to rotate.
**Step 2:** Identify the mismatch. Gliding joints are found in the wrist and ankle, not between the atlas and axis.

tips.text: A skeleton is a framework of about 206 bones that protects the body’s organs, supports the body, provides attachment points for muscles to enable body movement, functions as a storage site for minerals such as calcium and phosphorus, and produces blood cells.
The skeletal system is broadly divided into two parts: the axial and appendicular skeletons.
Bone is strong, hard and slightly elastic.
Although mature bones consist largely of calcium, most bones in the skeleton of humans begin as cartilage.
Bone has organic and inorganic parts; it is living tissue and is rich in blood vessels.
The various bones found in the body have different shapes and sizes to reflect the different functions they carry out.
Do bones work independent of each other? 2.
Why do you think we need of joints in our skeletal system? 3.
What is the significance of having movable and immovable joints?
A joint is the place where two bones fuse or come together. There are generally two types of joints, which are classified according to the amount of movement they allow.
Vertebrae: 7-12-5-5-4 (33 in a child, 26 bones in an adult). Ribs: 7 true, 3 false, 2 floating.

questions.q: The adult human vertebral column (spine) is made up of 33 vertebrae. Which of the following correctly matches each region of the spine with its number of vertebrae?
why: **Recall the total number of vertebrae.** The unit states that the vertebral column (spine) consists of 33 vertebrae separated by fibrocartilaginous intervertebral discs, and that it is divided into five regions.
**Assign the cervical and thoracic counts.** The cervical region contains 7 vertebrae, which include the atlas and axis that permit head rotation. The thoracic region contains 12 vertebrae.

**Assign the lumbar, sacral and caudal counts.** The lumbar region contains 5 vertebrae. The sacral region contains 5 fused vertebrae that form the sacrum, and the caudal (coccygeal) region contains 4 fused vertebrae that form the coccyx.

**Check the sum and select the matching option.** Adding the regions: 7 + 12 + 5 + 5 + 4 = 33, which agrees with the stated total. Option B wrongly gives 12 cervical and 7 thoracic vertebrae; option C wrongly gives 5 thoracic, 12 lumbar, 4 sacral and 5 caudal vertebrae; option D wrongly gives only 5 cervical and 7 lumbar vertebrae. Only option A is fully consistent with the unit.

questions.q: An anatomy chart in a school laboratory in Asmara lists 8 cranial bones and 14 facial bones. Calculate the total number of bones in the skull, and state the type of joint that fuses the cranial bones together.
questions.answer: The skull contains 22 bones (8 cranial + 14 facial), and the cranial bones are fused at immovable (fibrous) joints called sutures.
why: **Identify the two groups of skull bones.** The unit divides the skull into 8 cranial bones, which are fused together to protect the brain, and 14 facial bones, which form the architecture of the face and support the teeth.
**Add the two groups.** Total skull bones = 8 cranial + 14 facial = 22 bones.
**Name the joint type.** The cranial bones are joined at immovable fibrous joints called sutures, which allow zero movement in order to protect the delicate brain tissue.

questions.q: A vertebral column model in a biology laboratory in Keren has lost 3 of its thoracic vertebrae. How many vertebrae remain in the model, and how many of the remaining vertebrae are fused?
questions.answer: 30 vertebrae remain in the model, of which 9 are fused (5 sacral and 4 caudal).
why: **State the complete column.** A complete vertebral column contains 33 vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral and 4 fused caudal vertebrae.
**Subtract the lost thoracic vertebrae.** The model has lost 3 thoracic vertebrae, so the thoracic region now has 12 - 3 = 9 vertebrae and the whole column has 33 - 3 = 30 vertebrae.

**Count the fused vertebrae.** Only the sacral and caudal regions are fused: 5 sacral + 4 caudal = 9 fused vertebrae. These are unaffected by the loss of thoracic vertebrae, so 9 of the remaining 30 vertebrae are fused.

questions.q: A fresh long bone sample taken from a slaughtered ox at the abattoir in Asmara has a total mass of 480 g. In bone, the organic matrix makes up approximately $$\frac{1}{3}$$ of the total bone mass and the inorganic mineral salts make up the remaining $$\frac{2}{3}$$. (a) Calculate the mass of the organic matrix and the mass of the inorganic mineral salts in this sample. (b) The sample is then soaked in a weak acid (vinegar) for several days. State the mass of the sample that remains and describe its physical properties, giving the chemical reason for the change.
questions.answer: (a) Organic matrix = 160 g and inorganic mineral salts = 320 g. (b) 160 g of the sample remains; the bone becomes soft, flexible and rubbery because the acid dissolves the calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite) mineral matrix, leaving only the organic collagen matrix.
why: **Identify the composition fractions from the unit.** The unit states that the organic portion is approximately $$\frac{1}{3}$$ of total bone mass (collagen fibres, ground substance and bone cells) and that the inorganic mineral salts are the remaining $$\frac{2}{3}$$ (mainly calcium phosphate crystals in the form of hydroxyapatite).
**Calculate the mass of the organic matrix.** Organic mass = $$\frac{1}{3} \times 480\text{ g} = 160\text{ g}$$.
**Calculate the mass of the inorganic mineral salts.** Inorganic mass = $$\frac{2}{3} \times 480\text{ g} = 320\text{ g}$$. Check: 160 g + 320 g = 480 g, which equals the total mass of the sample.

**Work out the mass remaining after the acid soak.** The weak acid dissolves the inorganic mineral matrix (the calcium phosphate salts). Only the organic collagen matrix is left intact, so the remaining mass equals the organic mass, 160 g.

**Describe the physical change and conclude.** Because the hard, rigid mineral component that gives bone its compressional strength has been removed, the bone loses its hardness and rigidity and becomes highly flexible and rubbery, so it can be bent or twisted without breaking.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A bone sample of 300 g is baked in an oven at a high temperature for several hours. Using the composition $$\frac{1}{3}$$ organic and $$\frac{2}{3}$$ inorganic, calculate the mass of the sample that remains and describe its physical properties, explaining the chemical basis for the change.
questions.answer: 200 g of the sample remains; the bone becomes extremely brittle and chalky because the heat destroys (denatures) the organic collagen matrix, leaving only the inorganic mineral salts.
why: **State the composition of the sample.** The organic matrix is $$\frac{1}{3}$$ and the inorganic mineral salts are $$\frac{2}{3}$$ of bone mass, as given in the unit.

**Calculate the mass of organic matrix destroyed.** Organic mass = $$\frac{1}{3} \times 300\text{ g} = 100\text{ g}$$. High temperature denatures the collagen fibres and proteins, so this 100 g is destroyed.
**Calculate the mass remaining.** Remaining mass = 300 g - 100 g = 200 g, which is exactly the inorganic fraction $$\frac{2}{3} \times 300\text{ g} = 200\text{ g}$$ of mineral salts.

**Describe the physical result and conclude.** With the organic matrix gone, the bone loses its flexibility and tensile strength; only the hard mineral salts remain, so the bone becomes extremely brittle, chalky and easy to shatter under minimal pressure.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A dried bone sample from a butcher's shop in Keren is found to contain 210 g of inorganic mineral salts. If the inorganic salts make up $$\frac{2}{3}$$ of bone mass, calculate the total mass of the sample and the mass of its organic matrix.
questions.answer: The total mass of the sample is 315 g and its organic matrix is 105 g.
why: **Set up the fraction relationship.** The unit states that inorganic mineral salts form $$\frac{2}{3}$$ of total bone mass. Let the total mass be $$M$$, so $$\frac{2}{3}M = 210\text{ g}$$.
**Solve for the total mass.** Multiply both sides by $$\frac{3}{2}$$: $$M = 210 \times \frac{3}{2} = 315\text{ g}$$.
**Calculate the organic mass.** Organic mass = total mass - inorganic mass = 315 g - 210 g = 105 g. Check: $$\frac{1}{3} \times 315\text{ g} = 105\text{ g}$$, which agrees.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: In a Grade 11 biology laboratory in Nakfa, students assemble a model of the adult axial skeleton, which consists of the skull, the vertebral column and the thoracic cage. Using the numbers given in the unit, (a) calculate the total number of bones in the axial skeleton by adding the skull bones (8 cranial + 14 facial), the 33 vertebrae and the thoracic cage (1 sternum + 12 pairs of ribs); and (b) express this axial total as a percentage of the 206 bones of the adult skeleton, correct to one decimal place.
questions.answer: (a) The axial skeleton contains 80 bones. (b) This is $$\frac{80}{206} \times 100\% \approx 38.8\%$$ of the 206 bones of the adult skeleton.
why: **Count the skull bones.** The skull = 8 cranial bones + 14 facial bones = 22 bones.
**State the number of vertebrae.** The vertebral column contains 33 vertebrae (7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral and 4 fused caudal).
**Count the bones of the thoracic cage.** The thoracic cage = 1 sternum + 12 pairs of ribs = 1 + (12 $$\times$$ 2) = 1 + 24 = 25 bones.
**Add the three parts to obtain the axial total.** Axial skeleton = 22 + 33 + 25 = 80 bones. This agrees with the unit value of 80 bones for the axial skeleton.

**Express the axial total as a percentage of the whole skeleton.** Percentage = $$\frac{80}{206} \times 100\% = 38.8349\ldots\% \approx 38.8\%$$. Check: the appendicular skeleton is 206 - 80 = 126 bones, and $$\frac{126}{206} \times 100\% \approx 61.2\%$$, and 38.8% + 61.2% = 100%.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

(b) Express the bones of both lower limbs as a percentage of the 126 bones of the appendicular skeleton, correct to one decimal place.
questions.answer: (a) One lower limb has 30 bones, so both lower limbs have 60 bones. (b) $$\frac{60}{126} \times 100\% \approx 47.6\%$$ of the appendicular skeleton.
why: **List the single bones of one lower limb.** The unit lists the femur (thigh bone), the patella (kneecap), and the tibia and fibula (shin bones), which are 4 individual bones.
**Add the numbered groups of one lower limb.** One lower limb = 4 + 7 tarsals + 5 metatarsals + 14 phalanges = 4 + 7 + 5 + 14 = 30 bones.
**Calculate both lower limbs.** Both lower limbs = 2 $$\times$$ 30 = 60 bones.
**Express as a percentage of the appendicular skeleton.** Percentage = $$\frac{60}{126} \times 100\% = 47.6190\ldots\% \approx 47.6\%$$.

questions.q: The thoracic cage contains 12 pairs of ribs. The top 7 pairs are true ribs, the next 3 pairs are false ribs and the bottom 2 pairs are floating ribs. (a) Calculate the total number of individual ribs. (b) Calculate the percentage of the total ribs that are true ribs and the percentage that are floating ribs, each correct to one decimal place.
questions.answer: (a) There are 24 individual ribs. (b) True ribs = $$\frac{14}{24} \times 100\% \approx 58.3\%$$ and floating ribs = $$\frac{4}{24} \times 100\% \approx 16.7\%$$ of all ribs.
why: **Convert pairs of ribs into individual ribs.** 12 pairs of ribs = 12 $$\times$$ 2 = 24 individual ribs.
**Calculate the number of true ribs.** True ribs are the top 7 pairs, which connect directly to the sternum via their own costal cartilages: 7 $$\times$$ 2 = 14 ribs.
**Calculate the number of floating ribs.** Floating ribs are the bottom 2 pairs, which do not connect to the sternum at all: 2 $$\times$$ 2 = 4 ribs.

**Express each group as a percentage of 24 ribs.** True ribs: $$\frac{14}{24} \times 100\% = 58.333\ldots\% \approx 58.3\%$$. Floating ribs: $$\frac{4}{24} \times 100\% = 16.666\ldots\% \approx 16.7\%$$. The remaining 6 false ribs give $$\frac{6}{24} \times 100\% = 25.0\%$$, and 58.3% + 25.0% + 16.7% = 100%.

questions.q: A cyclist riding from Asmara down to Massawa falls from her bicycle and injures her knee. At the hospital the doctor explains that the knee is a freely movable joint. (a) Describe the structural features of a freely movable (synovial) joint and explain how these features prevent wear and tear on the articulating bone ends during high-impact movement. (b) Classify the elbow joint, the shoulder joint and the atlas-axis joint by their mechanical shape, and state the movement that each one permits.
questions.answer: (a) In a synovial joint the articulating bone ends are separated by a joint cavity filled with synovial fluid and enclosed by an articular capsule lined with a synovial membrane. Articular (hyaline) cartilage cushions the bone ends and absorbs compressional shock, while the synovial fluid lubricates the joint and reduces friction to near zero, so wear and tear are prevented. (b) The elbow is a hinge joint (flexion and extension in a single plane), the shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint (multidirectional rotation), and the atlas-axis joint is a pivot joint (rotation around a central axis).
why: **Define the freely movable joint.** A freely movable (synovial) joint is one in which the articulating bone ends are separated by a joint cavity filled with lubricating synovial fluid, and the whole joint is enclosed by a tough articular capsule lined with a synovial membrane.

**Explain the role of articular cartilage.** The bone ends are covered by a layer of articular (hyaline) cartilage. This cartilage cushions the bone ends, absorbs compressional shock and minimises friction between the moving surfaces.

**Explain the role of synovial fluid and the capsule.** The synovial membrane secretes synovial fluid into the joint cavity; this slippery fluid lubricates the joint and reduces friction to near zero, while the articular capsule holds the fluid in place and keeps the joint stable.
**Classify the elbow joint.** The elbow is a hinge joint, in which a convex surface fits into a concave depression, permitting flexion and extension in a single plane.

**Classify the shoulder and the atlas-axis joints.** The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint, in which a ball-like head fits into a cup-like socket, allowing rotational movement in multiple planes. The atlas-axis joint is a pivot joint, in which a rounded surface rotates within a ring, allowing rotation of the head around a central axis.

questions.q: A metalworker in Asmara can swing his arm freely in all directions, yet the bones of his skull cannot move at all. Compare the skull sutures and the shoulder joint in terms of the connective tissue that binds the bones, the range of movement allowed, and the protective or mechanical advantage each arrangement provides.
questions.answer: The skull sutures are immovable (fibrous) joints, bound tightly by dense, tough fibrous connective tissue, allowing zero movement so that the delicate brain is protected. The shoulder is a freely movable (synovial) ball-and-socket joint with a joint cavity, synovial fluid, an articular capsule and a synovial membrane, allowing rotational movement in multiple planes so that the arm can be used for mechanical work.
why: **Describe the immovable joint.** Immovable (fibrous) joints, such as the sutures of the skull, are bound together by dense, tough fibrous connective tissue and allow zero movement.
**State the advantage of the immovable joint.** Because no movement is possible, the fused skull bones form a rigid protective case for the delicate tissues of the brain.

**Describe the freely movable joint.** The shoulder is a freely movable (synovial) joint: the articulating bone ends are separated by a joint cavity filled with lubricating synovial fluid, enclosed by an articular capsule lined with a synovial membrane.

**State the mechanical advantage and conclude.** The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint, so a ball-like head fits into a cup-like socket and rotational movement in multiple planes is possible. This gives the arm a wide range of movement for lifting and manipulating objects, whereas the skull sutures give protection instead of mobility.

questions.q: A long-distance bus driver in Keren complains of stiffness and pain in his back. Explain how the type of joint between the vertebrae allows the spine to be both flexible and shock-absorbing, and contrast this with the joint that allows the head to turn from side to side.
questions.answer: The vertebrae are joined by slightly movable (cartilaginous) joints separated by fibrocartilaginous intervertebral discs, which permit limited, restricted movement so the spine is flexible and the discs absorb shock. The side-to-side turning of the head is produced by the pivot joint between the atlas and the axis, which allows rotation around a central axis.
why: **Identify the joint between the vertebrae.** The 33 vertebrae are separated by fibrocartilaginous intervertebral discs, making these slightly movable (cartilaginous) joints that are connected by resilient pads of cartilage.
**Explain the movement and shock absorption.** Slightly movable joints permit only limited, restricted movement; this gives the spine flexibility while the discs absorb shock and provide stability.

**Identify the joint used for turning the head.** The first two cervical vertebrae form the atlas-axis joint, which is a pivot joint in which a rounded surface rotates within a ring, allowing rotation around a central axis.

**Contrast the two joint types and conclude.** The vertebral joints are cartilaginous and allow only slight movement distributed along the column, whereas the atlas-axis pivot joint allows full rotation of the head. Neither joint is a freely movable synovial joint of the ball-and-socket kind.

questions.q: A 13-year-old student in Keren is told by a doctor that the long bones of her arms and legs are still elongating. (a) Explain how endochondral ossification at the epiphyseal plates allows a long bone to increase in length, naming the cells and processes involved. (b) Explain why elongation stops at skeletal maturity. (c) The unit states that approximately 10% of the entire adult skeleton is completely replaced every year by bone remodeling. Deduce the number of years required for a complete turnover of the skeleton, and name the two cell types responsible for remodeling and state the role of each.
questions.answer: (a) The embryonic cartilage model is invaded by blood vessels that deliver osteoblasts, which replace cartilage with mineralised bone, while at the epiphyseal plate chondrocytes divide on the cartilage side and osteoblasts replace the old cartilage with bone on the osseous side, so the bone elongates. (b) Elongation stops because the epiphyseal plates completely ossify at skeletal maturity, leaving no cartilage to be converted into bone. (c) A complete turnover of the skeleton takes $$\frac{100\%}{10\%} = 10\text{ years}$$; the two cell types are osteoblasts (which build and mineralise bone matrix) and osteoclasts (which dissolve bone minerals and digest collagen, releasing calcium).
why: **State the starting material of the embryonic skeleton.** During early fetal development the skeleton is composed almost entirely of flexible hyaline cartilage, and ossification is the process by which this embryonic cartilage is transformed into solid bone.

**Describe endochondral ossification.** In endochondral ossification, blood vessels invade the cartilage models and deliver osteoblasts, which gradually replace the cartilage with a hard mineralised matrix.

**Explain growth at the epiphyseal plate.** In children the epiphyseal plates (growth plates) lie between the shaft and the ends of long bones. Chondrocytes continuously divide on the cartilage side of the plate, while osteoblasts replace the old cartilage with bone on the osseous side, so the bone elongates.

**Explain why growth stops at skeletal maturity.** The plates continue to allow elongation only until they completely ossify at skeletal maturity. Once the plate has ossified there is no cartilage left for the chondrocytes to divide and for the osteoblasts to replace, so the bone can no longer increase in length.
**Calculate the time for complete skeletal turnover.** If 10% of the skeleton is replaced each year, then the time for a complete turnover is $$\frac{100\%}{10\%\text{ per year}} = 10\text{ years}$$.

**Name the remodeling cells and their roles.** Osteoblasts are bone-building cells that synthesise and deposit the organic osteoid matrix and facilitate its mineralisation. Osteoclasts are large, multinucleated bone-resorbing cells that secrete acids and enzymes to dissolve bone minerals and digest collagen, releasing calcium into the blood.

questions.q: A 15-year-old boy in Massawa fractures the shaft of his femur while playing football, and the doctor says the bone will heal rapidly. Explain why bone heals much faster than cartilage following physical trauma, referring to the blood supply and cells of each tissue.
questions.answer: Bone heals rapidly because it is highly vascular: the periosteum is rich in blood vessels and contains bone-forming osteoblasts, and the central canals and perforating canals deliver nutrients and cells directly to the injury site. Cartilage is entirely avascular and must rely on slow nutrient diffusion from the surrounding perichondrium, so it heals much more slowly.
why: **Describe the blood supply and cells of bone.** The unit states that the outer surface of a bone is covered by the periosteum, a fibrous membrane rich in blood vessels, nerves and bone-forming stem cells called osteoblasts, and that central canals and perforating canals carry vessels into the bone.

**Link this to rapid repair.** Because nutrients and osteoblasts are delivered directly to the fracture site by the rich blood supply, the bone matrix can be rebuilt quickly, which is why a fractured femur shaft heals rapidly.

**Describe the blood supply of cartilage.** Cartilage is entirely avascular (lacking blood vessels), so it must rely on slow nutrient diffusion from the surrounding tissues (perichondrium) to repair itself.

**Conclude the comparison.** The absence of a direct blood supply makes cartilage repair slow, whereas the highly vascular periosteum, central canals and perforating canals of bone make bone repair comparatively rapid.

questions.q: A child in Asmara suffers a disorder in which the epiphyseal plates of the long bones ossify completely at the age of 8 years instead of at skeletal maturity. Predict the effect on the length of the child's arms and legs, and explain the role of the growth plate in normal bone elongation, naming the cells involved.
questions.answer: The arms and legs will stop elongating at 8 years and the child will remain unusually short, because the epiphyseal plates have ossified and no cartilage remains. Normally chondrocytes divide on the cartilage side of the plate while osteoblasts replace the old cartilage with bone on the osseous side, so the bone keeps elongating until the plate ossifies at skeletal maturity.
why: **Recall the normal role of the epiphyseal plate.** The epiphyseal plates (growth plates) lie between the shaft and the ends of long bones; chondrocytes continuously divide on the cartilage side of the plate while osteoblasts replace the old cartilage with bone on the osseous side.
**Relate the plate to elongation.** This continuous division and replacement is what allows bones to elongate during childhood, so the arms and legs grow longer year by year.

**Apply the premature ossification.** If the plates ossify completely at 8 years, there is no cartilage left for chondrocytes to divide and no cartilage for osteoblasts to replace, so elongation of the long bones ceases permanently.

**State the predicted outcome.** The child's arms and legs will stop growing at 8 years and remain short, so the child will be unusually short, whereas normally elongation continues until the plates ossify at skeletal maturity.
